Impute Numeric Values from Character Results with Qualifiers

Source: R/compute_qual_imputation.R
compute_qual_imputation.Rd

Converts character results to numeric values, with an optional shift for strict inequality qualifiers.

Usage

compute_qual_imputation(
  character_value,
  imputation_type = "strip",
  factor = NULL,
  offset = 0
)

Arguments

character_value

Character vector of numeric results, optionally prefixed with a qualifier, for example, c("<40", ">=40.1", "3").

Default value

none

imputation_type

How to convert the character results:

  • "strip": Remove qualifiers and use offset as the additive offset for strict inequalities.

  • "shift": Remove qualifiers and use the decimal precision of each original character result as the additive offset. See Details.

  • 1 - equivalent to "strip".

  • 2 - equivalent to "shift".

Permitted values

"strip", "shift"

Default value

"strip"

factor

Deprecated alias for offset.

Default value

NULL

offset

Finite, nonnegative numeric scalar used when imputation_type = "strip". It is added for results with > and subtracted for results with <. It is ignored when imputation_type = "shift".

Default value

0

Value

A numeric vector of imputed results.

Details

Qualified results must match ^[<>]=?[0-9]+[.]?[0-9]*$, for example, "<40", ">=40.1", or ">40.". Unqualified decimal numbers, optionally signed, are also accepted, including "-3", "+3", and ".5". Whitespace, scientific notation, signed qualified values, and malformed qualifiers are not accepted. Invalid strings and missing values return NA_real_ without a warning. Results keep the input order and length.

For a strict > qualifier, add the offset; for a strict < qualifier, subtract it. Results with >= or <=, or without an inequality qualifier, are converted without a shift.

With imputation_type = "shift", the offset is \(10^{-d}\), where \(d\) is the number of decimal places in the original character result, including trailing zeros. For integer results, the offset is 1. For example, "<40" becomes 39, ">40.1" becomes 40.2, and ">40.10" becomes 40.11.

Numeric methods 1 and 2 are deprecated aliases for "strip" and "shift", respectively. Both still work and produce a deprecation message.

Choose an imputation rule that matches the analysis specification. A shift can cross zero, so results can be negative.

See also

BDS-Findings Functions that returns a vector: compute_bmi(), compute_bsa(), compute_egfr(), compute_framingham(), compute_map(), compute_qtc(), compute_qual_imputation_dec(), compute_rr(), compute_scale(), transform_range()

Examples

values <- c("<40", ">40.1", "<=40", ">=40.1", "3")
compute_qual_imputation(values)
#> [1] 40.0 40.1 40.0 40.1  3.0
compute_qual_imputation(values, offset = 0.5)
#> [1] 39.5 40.6 40.0 40.1  3.0
compute_qual_imputation(values, imputation_type = "shift")
#> [1] 39.0 40.2 40.0 40.1  3.0

# Trailing zeros retain the reported precision
compute_qual_imputation(c(">40.1", ">40.10"), imputation_type = "shift")
#> [1] 40.20 40.11

# Malformed qualifiers produce missing values without warnings
compute_qual_imputation(c("0>1", "-<0.9>", ">100.00", "<1"), "shift")
#> [1]     NA     NA 100.01   0.00
